title: What a hunting beetle could see, and what the ground hides
question: One cell of eye height turns a third of the blocked sight lines green. Which of these reads right for an insect hunting on a forest floor — eye on the deck, or eye a cell up?
context_md:
Sizing a sight sense before it is built (E15). Green = beetle can see that ant; dark red = the line is stopped by something; the red dot is the cell that stopped it.

**Most blocked lines are stopped at their first step**, by a seed or a leaf lying right beside the beetle — so they draw as a dot rather than a line, and blocking looks rarer in the picture than it is. The numbers below are the real count.

What I already measured, 18 world seeds: over the whole world, terrain stops **28%** of beetle-to-ant lines at eye level and **9%** one cell up. What stops them is litter, seeds, corpses and soil — floor clutter, not hills or trunks.

What I am unsure of is whether a beetle that sees over its own litter is right, or whether being blinded by the debris it walks through is the more satisfying animal.
